title: Work as Zen
hookLine: an old cook drying mushrooms in the hot sun: in Zen monasteries, the work period is practice too
last: KEEP THE BEGINNER'S MIND; DON'T GRADUATE FROM IT.

cards: Midday, a Chinese monastery, and the sun is brutal. An old monk with a bent back is out in the courtyard with no hat, spreading mushrooms to dry, sweating.

A visitor from Japan, Dogen, the same Dogen who began this week, stops and asks: why not have a helper do this? The old cook answers, in effect: other people are not me. And why not wait until it's cooler?
If not now, when? Dogen writes that he had nothing to say back. He tells the story in his instructions for the monastery cook.

teach.h: SAMU: THE WORK PERIOD AS PRACTICE.
teach.b: Samu is the Japanese Zen word for the work period: cleaning, cooking, sweeping, weeding, done as practice. Back on day forty-seven, Zhaozhou sent a monk to wash his bowl; samu builds that idea into the day.
First, what it is. In a Zen monastery the day isn't only sitting.
There are set times for physical work, treated as part of the training, not a break from it, often done without chatter, with the attention the cushion asks for. Second, an old saying.
Tradition says the Chinese teacher Baizhang kept working in the fields even when he was old. His worried students hid his tools.

teach.h: A DAY WITHOUT WORK, A DAY WITHOUT FOOD.
teach.b: He refused to eat, and said, as the story goes: a day without work is a day without food. Whether or not it happened just that way, Zen still repeats the saying.
Third, the cook's answer. Other people are not me. He wasn't refusing help out of pride.

His practice was this task, in his own hands; sending it away would send away his practice. And if not now, when: the moment to pay attention is the one you're in, even if it's hot. Fourth, off the cushion.

teach.h: THE CUSHION, WITH YOUR HANDS MOVING.
teach.b: Washing a pan can be zazen with your hands moving. In his instructions for the cook, Dogen asks, in paraphrase, that rice and water be handled with the care you'd give your own eyes.
Nobody has to live in a monastery to try that with a sink full of dishes.

how: In Zen monasteries and practice centers, residents keep a daily work period, cleaning, cooking or gardening, often in silence, as part of their training.

o: a fine paid by monks who skip their duties
the Zen work period: chores done as practice
a break from meditation to rest the body

games.q: you're the old cook. it's blazing hot, and a visitor suggests you hand the mushrooms to a helper or wait till it's cooler. what do you say?
o: other people are not me. if not now, when?
games.why: Dogen tells it in his instructions for the cook: the old man kept working, and Dogen had nothing to say back.

practice: Find one small thing within reach that needs care, a cup to wash, a table to wipe, a pair of shoes to line up, and do it slowly, feeling its weight, the water's temperature, the cloth under your hand.

When your mind runs ahead to what's next, come back to this one motion; if you can't move where you are, tidy one thing in your pocket or bag. Another day, ten minutes of cleaning this way is a good next step.

wordCard.voice: Samu. The Zen work period, cleaning, cooking, tending, done as practice, with the same attention as sitting. Today's word.

orig.note: Japanese: the Zen work period, work done as practice.

carryVoice: Your line: work is practice. Not someone else, and not later: this one, now. Rest easy.

sources.ref: the saying attributed to Baizhang Huaihai
